item.research_question: How can equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy be synthesized into complex shapes via additive manufacturing, and how can its oxidation resistance be improved for extreme temperature applications?
item.material_system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) synthesized from a blend of hydride powders (TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5) and elemental powders
item.processing_route: 3D ink-extrusion printing of inks containing hydride powders, de-binding under flowing H2 at 450 °C for 30 min, vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, and silicide coating via pack cementation at 950 °C for 24 h
item.test_conditions: Compression testing at 800–1100 °C with strain rates of 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) at 1000 °C under flowing air for 20 h; In situ X-ray diffraction from 100 to 1000 °C under vacuum
key_findings: Sequential decomposition of hydride powders occurs between 290 °C and 720 °C, following the order of hydride formation enthalpy (Ta, Nb, Ti, Hf, Zr).
Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h yields a nearly fully densified alloy with a relative density of 99.7 ± 0.2% and a linear shrinkage of 23.5 ± 0.1%.
Slow cooling after sintering produces a multiphase microstructure (β-BCC1 + β-BCC2 + α-HCP), whereas water quenching from 1500 °C yields a metastable single β-BCC phase.

The sintered bulk samples exhibit a yield strength significantly higher than arc-melted HfNbTaTiZr and Inconel 718 between 750 and 1100 °C, attributed to interstitial strengthening from ≈1.0 wt.% oxygen.
Silicide coating via pack cementation forms two distinct layers: a 40 ± 2 µm MSi2 layer (69 at.% Si) and a 5 ± 1 µm MSi layer (54 at.% Si).
The parabolic rate constant for oxidation at 1000 °C is 0.80 mg² cm⁻⁴ h⁻¹ for the silicide-coated sample, which is approximately 700 times lower than the uncoated sample (570 mg² cm⁻⁴ h⁻¹).
During oxidation, (Zr,Hf)O2 particles form within cracks in the silicide layer, effectively sealing them and preventing spallation, while Si diffuses deeper to expand the coating.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the high strength to interstitial solid-solution strengthening by oxygen and carbon, and the improved oxidation resistance to a self-healing mechanism where (Zr,Hf)O2 fills cracks in the silicide layer and Si diffusion expands the protective coating depth.
item.limitations: The sintered samples contain ≈1 wt.% oxygen and 0.102 wt.% carbon, which stabilize the α-HCP phase and raise the α-to-β transition temperature, preventing the formation of a single-phase microstructure without quenching. Additionally, cracks form in the silicide layer due to thermal expansion mismatch.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that active cooling by a fluid or filling the lattice core with a low-conductivity aerogel could further prevent cavity radiation and improve thermal insulation performance.
quotes: Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is synthesized.
The parabolic rate constant k is directly related to the self‐diffusion coefficient of oxygen (or metallic elements) in the oxide scale.
Thus, Zr and Hf within the silicide coating react with oxygen to form the oxide, while Si is released and diffuses deeper in the specimen.
